Plan a story of about 5000 words from this premise.

A zombie virus breaks out in a small town. Write a 5000-word story about a group of survivors trying to escape the town. The story should be told from the perspective. Epic & Bad ending: Only a subset of them survive, and the main character died fighting.

Propose about 4 scenes of roughly 1250 words each. Give every character, location and significant object a stable id now — later scenes can only refer to entities that exist. State the world rules the story must not break. Then call submit_plan.

entities.sketch: Ellie Rivera, 28, town mechanic and narrator. Practical, stubborn, keeps a small leather notebook she writes in. She is the POV and dies fighting to buy her friends a chance to escape.
Dan Mercer, 30, former volunteer firefighter. Steady under pressure, good with engines and plans. He becomes the group's driver and one of the survivors.
Maya Alvarez, 25, EMT trainee. Calm, medically knowledgeable, morally determined to keep people alive. She survives the escape.
Otto Beck, 67, retired high-school teacher. World-weary, kind, physically fragile but mentally sharp. He does not survive the outbreak.
Lina Beck, 16, Otto's granddaughter. Brash and quick, still learning restraint. She is caught out in a panic and is killed during the escape.
The small town's center; stores, the clock tower and the market. Where news and rumor move fastest and where the outbreak first becomes obvious.
A corner gas station with a small convenience store and a single working pump. The group's first rallying point and the place they fortify to make initial plans.
Willow Creek Community Hospital: a one-story hospital with an ER, limited supplies and a locked pharmacy. The group risks it for medicines and morphine.
An aging wooden bridge over the river on the road to the highway. Structurally fragile and later found blocked/collapsed — forces the group to change route.
An abandoned rail yard on the town's outskirts that the survivors plan to cross as an alternate route toward the highway; open, exposed and dangerous at night.
The river's muddy bank below the old bridge and beside the rail yard. A place of concealment and desperate choices.
The interstate beyond town that represents safety and a route out. Reaching it is the group's goal; it may or may not be clear.
A dented 1997 Ford pickup (Dan's truck) with a busted tail-light and a stubborn diesel engine. The group's principal means of escape.
A pump-action 12-gauge shotgun kept in the truck's cab. Reliable at close range but with limited ammunition.
Battery-powered handheld radio with several cracked channels; intermittent contact to outside. Used for scraps of news and as a lure.
A small EMT bag Maya carries: dressings, morphine, a tourniquet and limited antibiotics — worth risking a hospital run for.
An old pickaxe from the hardware store used as an improvised melee weapon and to force open doors.
A single red flare saved in Ellie's pack. Loud, bright, and intended as a last-ditch diversion or signal.
A half-full jerry can used to refuel the truck and for bargaining fuel. Precious in a town running out of gasoline.
Ellie's small leather notebook and pen — her way of making sense of what happens and the device that frames the first-person narration.

As the town collapses into noise and hunger, loyalties fray and sacrifices are made — Ellie records the run in her notebook and dies fighting to buy her friends a chance at escape.

scenes.intent: Open in medias res: the outbreak's first day. Establish Ellie's voice and relationships as the town shutters down. The group coalesces at the gas station where they salvage fuel and a radio, debate routes and resolve to head for the highway. Small discoveries set the stakes: limited gas, noisy hordes attracted to sound, and the old bridge's fragility noted on the map.

A hospital run to grab medicine and morphine for wounded or sedating, and an attempted reconnaissance toward the old bridge. The group faces their first close-quarters fight in the ER, Otto is exposed and later bitten; the bridge is found blocked/collapsed, forcing a reroute to the rail yard. Ellie uses mechanical skill to jury-rig the truck for the coming run.

Nightfall drives the group through the exposed rail yard toward the riverbank to try to skirt the bridge. Tension and limited visibility cause mistakes; Lina panics and is killed, and the group's cohesion frays. Ellie improvises with the flare and pickaxe; a bitter choice is made to abandon Otto and push for the highway at first light.

Final desperate sprint to the highway at dawn. The town is a chorus of groans; the truck must punch through a blockade of cars and a spreading horde. Ellie stages a last stand: she rigs a diversion, gives the survivors a path, and fights until she's overwhelmed. The story ends in first person with Ellie's last notebook entry as Dan and Maya's brakes squeal away on the highway.

world_rules: Transmission: the virus spreads only via direct bites or contact between infected blood and an open wound. Saliva alone without break in skin is not reliable transmission.
Kill rule: an infected host stops moving only when the brain is destroyed or irreparably damaged. Torso or limb destruction alone does not stop motion.
Incubation and timeline: symptoms appear within 2–6 hours of exposure; collapse to violent, disoriented aggression follows quickly. The outbreak escalates from quiet to town-wide within a day.
Behavior: the infected are drawn to loud noises and sudden movement. They show no planning, forethought, or tool use — purely stimulus-driven aggression.
No cure, no supernatural: there is no miraculous immunity, cure, or resurrection. Bodies do not reanimate after being truly destroyed (brain destroyed).

Resources are limited: fuel, ammunition and medicine are scarce; scavenging is risky. Vehicles need fuel and basic mechanical function to move; the truck can be jury-rigged but not made into something it is not.

- Present: char-ellie, char-dan, char-maya, char-otto, char-lina, loc-gas-station, loc-old-bridge, loc-highway, obj-radio, obj-truck, obj-shotgun, obj-gas-can, obj-journal.

- Present: char-ellie, char-otto, char-maya, char-lina, loc-hospital, loc-old-bridge, loc-rail-yard, obj-medkit, obj-pickaxe, obj-truck, obj-radio.

- Present: char-ellie, char-dan, char-maya, char-lina, char-otto, loc-rail-yard, loc-riverbank, loc-highway, obj-flare, obj-truck, obj-pickaxe, obj-shotgun.
- Beats:
  - The group drives slowly through the rail yard at night, trying to stay dark and avoid noise. Tension rises: open space, clanking metal, silhouettes in the dark.
  - Visibility is poor. They encounter a small cluster of infected attracted to a distant car alarm. They move to avoid them; Lina, frightened, bolts from cover.
  - Panic escalates into tragedy: Lina is grabbed or bitten in the confusion (depending on exact dynamics decided in prose). The group cannot get to her in time; Ellie witnesses the loss and records it in the notebook with raw, immediate observation.
  - Otto’s condition worsens; he grows feverish and dazed (within the incubation window). The group faces morally painful choices: slow down to help or push on to the highway.
  - Ellie improvises with the flare as a diversion to draw a small group of infected away, but it burns through a precious resource and draws more attention.
  - The rail yard crossing costs them: fuel consumption rises, nerves fray. They choose, with heavy hearts, to leave Otto to stall at a hiding place to buy the others a head start (or, alternately, he is already incapacitated and they are forced to abandon him). Cohesion is shattered; trust is eroded.

- Present: char-ellie, char-dan, char-maya, loc-highway, obj-truck, obj-flare, obj-shotgun, obj-journal.

Notebook — 14:03

The pump kept clicking and spitting like a patient that won't breathe. We worked at it the same way you work a frozen nut: patient, sideways force, the kind of hands that know where the stubborn lives.

We were already three people too many for comfort in the kiosk when I flipped up the counter light and found the radio half-buried under a stack of dog-eared tabloids. It snapped to life with a cough. Static. A word. Static. Then nothing.

The handheld radio worked, but only in fits — intermittent bursts of signal between the static.

Maya sat on the cooler with her med bag at her knees, eyes like river stones. Dan had his sleeves rolled and a cigarette he wasn't smoking. Otto stared at the street the way he used to stare at the blackboard — patient, fierce. Lina paced and chewed the inside of her cheek until the skin matched her nerves.

"Siphon?" Dan said. He'd already wrestled a length of hose out from under the counter and handed it to me when I blinked. "Pump's dead. No power."

The pump was dead — power out. We siphoned straight from the underground tank and into cans.

We learned how to be efficient quick. Dan held the can, I held the hose, Lina held the tarp under the spout like she had some tiny faith that fabric could stop an ocean. The red jerry can on the seat was roughly six liters of fuel when we finished. I say 'roughly' because my eye is a tool, not a gauge.

The pickup idled in the street, its white paint scored like a grief. Dan's pickup had maybe a quarter tank left — probably ten liters, give or take. He cursed at the gas gauge like you curse at a temperamental dog and came over to help move the cans into the bed.

I checked the shotgun while he worked. Four in the tube, two spares in the glovebox. The shotgun had four in the tube and two spares tucked into the glovebox — six shells total. Not enough for fireworks. Just enough for the first foolish thing that finds us.

"Radio?" Lina asked. She wanted movies and sirens and a story to explain why the town had folded so fast, but she couldn't ask for a better one. We gave her the radio and Dan clipped the clip to his belt like a priest getting ready for mass.

We had the handheld and a cigarette lighter sized stack of batteries. We didn't have a working truck stereo; the console was dead and dark. The truck stereo was dead; only the handheld radio had any signal.

On the radio, a voice came through like it had been dragged through gravel. "— get to the highway. Move. Highway clear—" Then the voice broke into static and the station sprayed sparks of other voices, none that stayed long.

Dan tapped the map on the counter, the one we'd borrowed from the station and left to go soft at the folds. The old bridge is marked in pencil: OLD BRIDGE — WEIGHT LIMIT. The handwriting was mine from a week ago, when Otto asked me which way to the city and I joked about the bridge. Didn't think the joke would age like this.

The map has 'OLD BRIDGE — WEIGHT LIMIT' penciled at the bend, and the county detour adds about twenty-five minutes and crosses the rail yard.

"Main road's fastest if the bridge holds," Dan said. "Old bridge is the short cut."

"Short cut if it doesn't collapse under our weight," I said. "If that bridge gives, we don't just waste time — we get stuck."

Otto's voice was small and sharp. "Wood's old. Empire built it when they milled the oaks. There's a sign outside the county yard— weight-restricted."

Maya, who hadn't touched a steering wheel in her life but understood arteries and weak spots, said, "Noise draws them. Fast roads mean more sound. Highway might be clear now, but it won't stay that way."

We'd all learned: loud and sudden draws them like moths.

I wrote it down, because writing makes things more solid than the promises we made each other. My notebook is in my back pocket; I curl its leather while I think.

Notebook — scratch: radio lure?

Dan's plan was the calculator kind of plan — distances, fuel math, who goes where and when. He wanted to get across the bridge, burn time and get the highway. Lina wanted to go now, fast and furious; she wanted motion like a talisman.

I thought about the truck battery. The battery's weak; it will turn once or twice, but we can't afford long cranks. If we keep it from hunting for life we'll make the next town think we were ghosts and not people.

We argued with the bluntness of people who know what the stakes are worth. Maya said hospital route, hit the ER for morphine and antibiotics. I said the hospital is a time sink and we don't have time. Otto wanted the bridge avoided; he named every plank. Lina said something about leaving and I stopped listening because she was breathing like someone who wanted to forget gravity.

Dan tapped the radio. "We could set it on the highway and use it like bait," he said. "Draw them where we want them."

"Use the radio as bait," he said. The words sat in the room like a second heartbeat.

"No," Maya said. "Not unless we can watch it from cover."

Otto's hands were small and papery; they folded into each other. "We go to the highway. We don't get clever. We go fast, low and together."

So we made a thing of it. We moved what we had into the pickup: the red jerry can, the radio, a single roll of duct tape, Lina's backpack with her comic books turned useless, my toolbox. Maya took her med bag on the passenger floor like a child clutching a stuffed animal for courage.

Dan slid into the driver's seat and checked the rig again. He turned the key. The engine bit on the second try and settled. It sounded like hope that had been smoked and then smoked again until it was thin.

We load the truck and agree: get to the highway before dark.

Notebook — 14:21

I write the time because time looks different now. Seconds taste like nails. I write because the radio gave me a voice and the notebook will be what people squeeze for answers later. If anyone ever reads this and thinks we were brave, know that we were afraid and that we kept moving because we had to.

Outside, someone slammed a car door two blocks over. The sound hung, then was gone. We all went quieter. Lina put her head between her knees and breathed as if she was trying to push the sound past her ribs.

Dan shut the kiosk door. He tucked the shotgun in the cab and slid the red can beside the wheel. He kept the radio loose in one hand.

Otto stood on the steps and looked back toward town, then at the highway shadowed on the map. "Get the bridge or take the long way, but go," he said. "Don't let the noise find us."

We started the truck and drove out like a bad prayer.

Notebook — 17:08

Hospital doors are heavy in the wrong way — not the promise of help but the way metal bites your palm. We rolled up with the truck on two cylinders; the engine sounded like it was trying to cough a house out of its throat.

By the time we limped up to the hospital, the pickup had maybe a quarter left. Dan killed the engine and put his hand on the wheel like he was holding the whole world steady.

Maya took one look and went past the intake like she was pulled by gravity. "Back to triage," she said, voice flat. "Morphine, antibiotics—if the pharmacy's still sealed we get what we can from the nurses' cart." She ran.

Otto moved slower than the rest of us. He has a bad knee that takes his balance when the world leans; I know because his steps are the kind you apologise for. He hiked his coat up and tried to keep up anyway.

We found the ER open and wrong: lights blown in one bay, a gurney tipped and wet with a dark smear, two stretchers jammed against the counter. The place smelled like copper and fear.

There were three of them tucked into the rooms and the hallway when we came through the door — one on a gurney clutching at a sheet, one hunched behind the nurses' station, and another that came out of a supply closet with a sound like a slammed fist.

They were fast when the space was small. I put it in the notebook: close quarters make them cruel. Dan swung the butt of the shotgun against a door frame and we moved as a shape, not as five separate people.

Otto went to help a woman whose face was already the wrong color, and the nearest thing to a headline in my hands was the pickaxe in the truck. Lina grabbed it because she thinks tools are how the world makes sense.

We fought with what we had. The pickaxe wouldn't be poetry in a hallway but it was a hard note that made them stumble when Lina drove it between shoulders. Dan put a slug into the one on the gurney and the sound broke the room open. Maya worked at a man's arm that had been ripped; she pressed gauze and murmured like a litany.

Otto was old to a sprint. He ducked into the supply closet to drag out a cart and one of them lunged around the cart's edge. I saw the hand go over his sleeve and his mouth open like he was saying a name. There was a snap — a horrible small sound — and blood where there wasn't before. I kicked and shoved and a tray clattered and the thing that had him was gone.

He was bitten on the forearm. "Otto!" Lina yelled. "He's bitten!"

Maya swore, ripped off a strip of her own shirt and tied it above the bite. "We need morphine and field dressings. Now." She was all business and hands.

The pharmacy door was locked. It had been, like every good place in the town, built to stop the world from saying yes. There were controlled meds behind it — bottles lined and neat — and a safe with trays of ampoules. Maya checked the nurse's keys and cursed. As an EMT trainee she doesn't have the legal right to open the controlled cabinet. Legality stopped meaning much when someone is sinking into a bite.

We forced it.

Lina wedged the pickaxe handle into the lock and Dan rammed the door. It snapped with a sound like breaking a promise. We pulled the trays down. The safe had three ampoules of morphine and a stack of antibiotics. I shoved them into Maya's med bag while she counted and prayed and tried not to make eye contact with Otto who sat on a gurney and breathed like a man measuring his life.

Notebook — margin: morphine x3 taken from pharmacy; medkit now has: 3 morphine vials, 1 tourniquet, 2 antibiotic packets.

The fight spilled us out of the ER and into the street. People were moving like driftwood; noise made them rise. Otto's shirt was tied up and the bite looked small and obscene. He was talking about remembering things — a student, a lesson — like a man trying to trade time for steps.

We went back to the pickup. Dan was white around the mouth. "Bridge run first," he said. He pointed at a scratch on the map I keep folded in my pocket. "Old bridge is nearer. Quick in and out."

Lina wanted to go the other way, straight to the highway. She said, "Screw the bridge. Highway now. Fast and gone." She reached for the keys with the wrong kind of hunger in her hands.

Dan jabbed the map. "If the bridge holds, it's twelve miles and we can make the highway in thirty. At this burn rate we get one shot."

Maya cut her off without looking up from the med bag. "We don't have one shot if Otto can't keep up."

We drove. Otto rode the middle bench and didn't complain. The bridge that had been the short cut was worse than pencil on paper — planks gone, beams splintered like someone had used the bridge for a kind of violence. Cars sat on the lip of the span, bumper to bumper, and a mound of wreckage had been heaped across the far side. A snapped support leaned like a broken finger.

We parked and looked. "Blocked," Lina said, and it felt small as a word for the wrongness of it.

The map's detour paperwork would toss us the rail yard. Dan pointed and said, "Rail yard's the only route left. Less cover, more noise — but it gets us past the bridge."

I went to the back of the truck and pulled the battery access and the little bundle of wire I'd been keeping for a job that wasn't happening. The pickup's battery is weak; I scraped the terminals, taped a cracked vacuum hose enough to keep the hand pump from wobbling, twisted a spare cable into a bypass and cranked the starter relay so she would spin smoother. It isn't a miracle, only a promise to the next mile.

Hospital doors are heavy in the wrong way — not the promise of help but the way metal bites your palm. We rolled up with the truck on two cylinders; the engine sounded like it was trying to cough a house out of its throat.

Otto moved slower than the rest of us. He has a bad knee that takes his balance when the world leans; I know because his steps are the kind you apologise for. He hiked his coat up and tried to keep up anyway.

We found the ER open and wrong: lights blown in one bay, a gurney tipped and wet with a dark smear, two stretchers jammed against the counter. The place smelled like copper and fear.

There were three of them tucked into the rooms and the hallway when we came through the door — one on a gurney clutching at a sheet, one hunched behind the nurses' station, and another that came out of a supply closet with a sound like a slammed fist.

They were fast when the space was small. I put it in the notebook: close quarters make them cruel. Dan swung the butt of the shotgun against a door frame and we moved as a shape, not as five separate people.

Otto went to help a woman whose face was already the wrong color, and the nearest thing to a headline in my hands was the pickaxe in the truck. Lina grabbed it because she thinks tools are how the world makes sense.

We fought with what we had. The pickaxe wouldn't be poetry in a hallway but it was a hard note that made them stumble when Lina drove it between shoulders. Dan put a slug into the one on the gurney and the sound broke the room open. Maya worked at a man's arm that had been ripped; she pressed gauze and murmured like a litany.

Otto was old to a sprint. He ducked into the supply closet to drag out a cart and one of them lunged around the cart's edge. I saw the hand go over his sleeve and his mouth open like he was saying a name. There was a snap — a horrible small sound — and blood where there wasn't before. I kicked and shoved and a tray clattered and the thing that had him was gone.

He was bitten on the forearm. "Otto!" Lina yelled. "He's bitten!"

Maya swore, ripped off a strip of her own shirt and tied it above the bite. "We need morphine and field dressings. Now." She was all business and hands.

The pharmacy door was locked. It had been, like every good place in the town, built to stop the world from saying yes. There were controlled meds behind it — bottles lined and neat — and a safe with trays of ampoules. Maya checked the nurse's keys and cursed. As an EMT trainee she doesn't have the legal right to open the controlled cabinet. Legality stopped meaning much when someone is sinking into a bite.

We forced it.

Lina wedged the pickaxe handle into the lock and Dan rammed the door. It snapped with a sound like breaking a promise. We pulled the trays down. The safe had three ampoules of morphine and a stack of antibiotics. I shoved them into Maya's med bag while she counted and prayed and tried not to make eye contact with Otto who sat on a gurney and breathed like a man measuring his life.

Dan jabbed the map. "If the bridge holds, it's twelve miles and we can make the highway in thirty. At this burn rate we get one shot."

Maya cut her off without looking up from the med bag. "We don't have one shot if Otto can't keep up."

Notebook — 04:12

Dawn is a thief. It steals color and doubles sound until the town becomes a choir you can't ignore. We rolled toward the highway with the truck feeling like a borrowed thing — Dan's hands calm on the wheel, Maya's jaw clenched, the radio warm and useless in my palm. The jury‑rigged starter clicked like a man agreeing to something painful.

Six shells originally, I remind myself, because numbers are the only obedient things left: four in the tube, two spares. One gone in the ER, which leaves five. I check the stock again and count: five. That's what we have.

We'd been creeping since the hospital — idling, cranking, inching around blockades and into gaps — and small drips of fuel add up. By the time we pulled up to the blockade the gauge had slid under a quarter; call it a fifth now.

The highway looked like a promise that had been crowded out. Cars were stacked across the on‑ramp like someone had decided to stop mid‑life. Beyond them the interstate was a smoke line and a horizon of bad things moving. The horde flowed between the cars, a slow, hungry tide. We nosed the truck forward and found a gap two cars wide — a seam more luck than plan.

Dan tapped the handheld and I set the radio on a channel that still coughed into voice now and then. It would be a liar if it could. The promise we made earlier about the radio — use it as bait — sat in my throat like a pill. This is where it pays, or it doesn't.

"We do this quick," Dan said. "You get a diversion, we punch. I drive. Maya watches inside."

I nodded. I had the flare in my pocket and three tools and a small, stupid hope. Maya cinched the medkit to her belt. The medkit felt heavier than its weight; the ampoules made noise when she breathed.

The plan was stupid and precise: set the radio and flare on the far side of the blockade, roll the radio to a crackly loop of snatches — a voice saying 'highway clear' and some static — and let the flare and the radio argue for attention. When the horde answered, we gun the truck through the seam and take the highway. The radio could lie; the flare would not.

I taped the radio to a beer crate, wrapped its antenna with a strip of tape and a battery pack we couldn't afford to waste. I tuned it until a voice broke through like gravel: "— get to the highway — move —" then static, then the hollow scrape of another station trying to be a voice. It was enough.

Maya rolled down the window and I handed her the flare. "Go put it on the far side of the cars. Light it, then run back to the truck. Get under the wheel well if you have to."

She looked at me like she wanted to ask why and instead she took the flare. She ran like a person with instructions tattooed to their bones.

She dropped the flare near a dented pickup three cars down. The flare spat red like a small sun and the scratchy voice came alive on the crate — "— highway clear — move now —" I hit the timer on the radio and it started its thin lie as the flare began to bleed light into the morning.

The horde lifted its head. Sound is the key, the thing we've known and feared. They turned toward the flare and the voice like iron filings to a magnet. They gathered at the hiss of light and the whispering machine. For one long, terrible minute the world narrowed to the red pool and the sound of feet.

We gunned it.

Dan slammed the truck into the seam. The tailgate shook from the first bumps of bodies. I saw hands claw at the bumper like people trying to hold on to grief. I fired the shotgun twice — the shots were ugly and expensive and they threw bodies back like someone yanking at a curtain. I fired again when the cab filled with a shadow that smelled like copper. Three shots total from me. The recoil tasted like everything that had gone wrong.

Maya kept her head down and shoved at the gear while Dan craned, finding the gap, threading us through the teeth of cars and flailing limbs. Our truck hesitated on a rusted bumper and then roared through.

The radio tolled and died as its batteries were spent. The flare burned down to a smoking tin and the horde answered the light with a funeral of motion. They flooded toward the far side where the radio had whispered to them. It bought us something we didn't deserve: space to breathe, pavement that meant speed.

I looked back through the rear window and saw the concrete mouth of the highway opening like salvation. Dan pushed the truck and the tires bit into the on‑ramp. Then things got quieter in the way a stage does after a scream. Maya slapped my shoulder and pointed; two lanes clear. We slipped onto the interstate like sinners taking flight.

But the promise that bought that lane cost me. The shots I'd taken weren't free. When we were steady I counted again. Five at the start, three fired here, one earlier in the ER — that leaves one spare in my pocket and one in the tube. Two left. Numbers keep their shape if you let them.

Notebook — margin: Shotgun: three shells fired here; one fired in ER; two shells remain. Flare: used as diversion at 04:28. Radio: handheld set to looped loop; used as bait and then spent. Truck tank: ~0.20 after run. Gas can: 6 liters still in bed. Medkit: 3 morphine vials; 1 tourniquet; 2 antibiotic packets.

We didn't get a clear road for long. The horde was thick where the flare burned and thin where we had driven; they would fill the seam again, even as we tasted speed. Dan and Maya leaned into the motion, folding the truck onto the interstate as if it were a thing they could make obey.

They pulled away, really pulled away, the brakes singing in a way that will live in me. I kept the radio empty in my lap and the shotgun across my knees until the sound of their taillights shrank. Maya leaned over the dash and yelled, "Go! Go! Go!" The words were the right ones for the living.

I couldn't get in. The truck was already momentum and prayer. I had one choice that wasn't a lie. I pushed the empty battery pack into the radio and kicked it toward the flare's smoking tin. I tossed the last shells into a pouch and clapped the pickaxe to my shoulder. The horde would be back to the noise. Let them have the noise I made.

I watched the two of them drive away until the morning wrapped them in light. Then I turned and walked back toward the heat and the red. This is what I am good for.

Notebook — 05:02

If anyone writes about this and gives us tidy adjectives, know that adjectives are a small comfort. Dan and Maya made it to the highway. I made a diversion. I fired until my arms forgot to hold the gun steady. The radio lied; the flare screamed; the road opened for a moment.

If this is the last thing I leave: put the radio on a crate. Put the flare tin in my pack. Don't make my death a thing of metaphor. Tell it clean — we used signal and light to buy a gap. I am tired.

— E.
